title: Trauma-informed care in everyday sessions
summary: Turning trauma-informed principles (safety, trustworthiness and transparency, peer support, collaboration, empowerment and choice, and attention to culture, history and gender) into concrete session behaviors. This is a way of working with everyone; it is different from trauma-focused therapy.
whenToUse: With every client, since a history of trauma is common and often not disclosed.
During assessment, physical or sensitive questions, and any procedure the client does not control.
When a client becomes distressed, shuts down or seems far away in session.

steps.heading: Safety
steps.body: Make the space predictable: explain what will happen, who else is around, where the exits are, and that the client can pause or stop at any time.

steps.heading: Trustworthiness and transparency
steps.body: Explain why you ask each kind of question before asking it, and what happens with the answers. Keep your word on time and follow-up.

steps.heading: Choice and collaboration
items: Offer choices about seating, pace, topics and how much to share.
Let the client control the pace of any disclosure; details are not needed to help.

steps.heading: Responding to a disclosure
items: Thank them for telling you, and believe them.
Say it was not their fault where that fits.
Ask what they need right now.
Explain any reporting duties honestly and before more detail if possible.
Check how they are feeling before the session ends.

steps.heading: Grounding when distress rises
steps.body: If a client becomes very distressed or disconnected, pause the topic, orient to the present (the room, the date, their feet on the floor), and use a grounding skill. Return to the topic only if they choose.

steps.heading: Culture, history and gender
steps.body: Ask how culture, identity and past experiences with services shape what feels safe, including historical and community trauma.

prompts: I am going to ask some questions about difficult experiences. You can answer as much or as little as you like, and we can stop at any time.
Thank you for telling me. That took courage. What you went through was not your fault.
You seem far away right now. Can you feel your feet on the floor? Tell me three things you can see in this room.
Is there anything that would make this space feel safer for you?
cautions: Trauma-informed care is not trauma-focused treatment. Do not start trauma processing without training and a plan.
Avoid suggestive questioning about possible forgotten trauma; memory can be shaped by suggestion.
Routine single-session debriefing soon after a trauma is not recommended and may cause harm.
Do not push for details; it can retraumatize and is rarely needed for care.
Mandatory reporting duties may apply to some disclosures; know them before you start.

adaptations.adaptation: Check the client is somewhere private and safe, agree on a signal to pause, and keep grounding skills ready for video.
Offer choice about the clinician's gender where possible, and be especially careful with touch, closed doors and positioning.

evidenceSummary: SAMHSA TIP 57 (2014) describes trauma-informed care in behavioral health services, including the principles used here and trauma-informed screening and assessment. A 2018 review (Sweeney and colleagues) describes how trauma-informed approaches change relationships in mental health services. NICE guideline NG116 (2018) advises against routine single-session psychological debriefing after trauma.
